title: Leaders Notice the Smallest Changes in People
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that personal change is hard and incremental, so good leaders watch for the earliest signs of effort rather than waiting for a finished result. Examples include a habitual meeting dominator who asks a question and then waits, or a last-minute manager who sends a draft two days early. Because early progress feels fragile and people quietly wonder whether anyone sees it, a leader who notices and names the change quickly and specifically removes doubt and signals hope that it will last. The note adds that small changes rarely earn praise, which is why recognition arrives when people are most tempted to give up. It closes by calling the practice one that costs the leader only attention, and invites teams to discuss how to spot early signs of change.
points: The best leaders watch for the smallest steps and earliest signs of effort instead of waiting for the finished product.
Early progress is fragile, and a leader who notices it dispels the doubt people quietly feel about whether anyone sees their effort.
Specific, prompt acknowledgment proves the leader was paying attention and points to a change most others would miss.
Noticing arrives at the moment people are most likely to give up, turning a solitary effort into a shared commitment.
The practice costs only attention yet often decides whether a new behaviour fades or becomes a habit.
quotes: The best leaders don’t wait for the finished product. They watch for the smallest steps and the earliest signs of effort and progress.
Early progress feels fragile, and people quietly wonder whether the effort is worth it and whether anyone sees it. When a leader notices, doubt loses its grip.
Leaders who notice the smallest change tell people what they have observed. They do it quickly and with precision.
Specificity proves the leader was paying attention and points to a change most others wouldn’t see.
While the timing is never perfect, noticing often reaches people at the exact moment they are most likely to give up. Small changes rarely earn praise, which makes the effort harder to sustain.
When a leader names what they saw, the effort becomes real to someone other than the person making it. The change is no longer a solitary act but a shared commitment.
Noticing the smallest changes costs leaders nothing but attention, yet it often decides whether a new behavior fades or becomes a habit.
